# Overview

Among other things, the multifactor package provides a set of tools to calculate
coverage and estimate enrichment for relational datasets. This type of operation 
forms the basis for bioinformatics techniques such as pathway enrichment 
analysis (PEA), but have application far beyond the biological sciences. 

## Setup 

```{r 'setup-multifactor', message = FALSE}
library(multifactor)

# Wrangling
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggforce)
library(systemfonts)
library(ragg)

# Define utility function
split_to_letters <- function(x) unique(
  unlist(
    strsplit(gsub(" ", "", x), split = ""),
    recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

### Example Dataset: The Quick Brown Fox 

We will use a toy data set of hierarchically structured data, namely the 
sentence: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' This sentence is a 
pangram, meaning that all 26 letters of the English alphabet are represented. 
Moreover, we have deconstructed the sentence to three levels; letters, words and
constituents. 

```{r 'load-qbf'}
# Load the quick brown fox data set
set.seed(2612)
fox <- quickbrownfox()
```

We could represent these relations visually like so:

```{r 'prep-plots', echo = FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, dev='ragg_png'}
word_lvs <- c("the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps", "over", "lazy", "dog")
cons_lvs <- c("subject", "predicate", "object")

letter2word_df <- as.data.frame(fox$letter2word) %>%
  mutate(
    word = factor(word, levels = word_lvs),
    label = "X"
  ) %>%
  arrange(word)

word2constituent_df <- as.data.frame(fox$word2constituent) %>%
  mutate(
    word = factor(word, levels = word_lvs),
    constituent = factor(constituent, levels = cons_lvs),
    label = "X"
  ) %>%
  arrange(constituent, word)


lm1 <- ggplot(letter2word_df) +
  geom_text(label = "X", x = I(0.5), y = I(0.5)) +
  ggtitle("Words to letters") +
  facet_grid(word ~ letter, switch = "y", space = "free_x")


lm2 <- ggplot(word2constituent_df) +
  geom_text(label = "X", x = I(0.5), y = I(0.5)) +
  ggtitle("Words to Constituents") +
  facet_grid(word ~ constituent, switch = "y", space = "free_x")

d <- "
AAAAAA
BBCCCC"

lm1 + lm2 + plot_spacer() +
  plot_layout(
    axes = "collect", axis_titles = "collect",
    nrow = 2L, design = d
  ) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") &
  theme_bw() &
  theme(
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0),
    panel.spacing = unit(0.1, "lines")
  )
```


```{r}
#| prep-coverage-plot, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE
input <- split_to_letters("a pangram is a sentence with all letters")

.mf_as_long <- function(x) bind_rows(
    lapply(
        S7::S7_data(x),
        function(i) dplyr::reframe(
            as.data.frame(i),
            from = i[[1L]], to = i[[2L]],
            from_y = as.integer(from), to_y = as.integer(to)
        )
    ) ,
    .id = "linkmap"
)

dfs <-lapply(
    S7::S7_data(fox),
    function(i) dplyr::reframe(
        as.data.frame(i),
        from = i[[1L]], to = i[[2L]],
        from_y = as.integer(from), to_y = as.integer(to)
    ))

word_colours <- c(
    "the"   = "#e41a1c",
    "quick" = "#377eb8",
    "brown" = "#a65628",
    "fox"   = "#4daf4a",
    "jumps" = "#984ea3",
    "over"  = "#ff7f00",
    "lazy"  = "#ffff33",
    "dog"   = "#f781bf"
)


letter2word <- mutate(
    dfs[[1]],
    from_y = 27-from_y,
    to_y = as.integer(
        factor(
            to,
            levels = rev(c(
                "the", "quick", "brown", "fox",
                "jumps", "over", "lazy", "dog"
            )))
    ),
    from_y = (from_y - mean(unique(from_y))) *
        (length(letters) / length(unique(from))),
    to_y = (to_y - mean(unique(to_y))) *
        (length(letters) / length(unique(to))),
    observed = from %in% input
) |>
    mutate(
        obs = sum(observed),
        tot = length(unique(from)),
        complete = obs == tot, .by = to
    )

word2constituent <- mutate(
    dfs[[2]],
    from_y = letter2word[["to_y"]][match(from, letter2word[["to"]])],
    
    to_y = (to_y - mean(unique(to_y))) *
        (length(letters) / length(unique(to)))
) |> left_join(
    dplyr::select(letter2word, from = to, obs, tot, l = from, observed, complete), 
    by = "from",relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(tot_con = length(unique(l)),
           obs_con1 = length(unique(l)[observed]),
           obs_con2 = length(unique(l)[complete]),
           obs_con3 = length(unique(l)[observed & obs > (tot/2)]),
           .by = to) |>
    dplyr::select(-l) |>
    distinct()

constituent2sentence <- mutate(
    dfs[[3]],
    to = to |>
        str_replace("brown fox", "brown\nfox") |>
        str_replace("over the", "over\nthe"),
    from_y = (from_y - mean(unique(from_y))) *
        (length(letters) / length(unique(from))),
    to_y = (to_y - mean(unique(to_y))) *
        (length(letters) / length(unique(to)))
)


pstart <- ggplot() +

    ggforce::geom_link(
        data = word2constituent,
        aes(y = from_y, yend = to_y, x = 1.5, xend = 2.5),
        linewidth = 2,
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    ggforce::geom_link(
        data = word2constituent,
        aes(y = from_y, yend = to_y, x = 1.5, xend = 2.5, colour = from),
        linewidth = 1,
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    
    ggforce::geom_diagonal(
        data = letter2word,
        aes(y = from_y, yend = to_y, x = 0, xend = 1.5),
        linewidth = 2,
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    ggforce::geom_diagonal(
        data = letter2word,
        aes(x = 0, xend = 1.5, y = from_y, yend = to_y, colour = to),
        linewidth = 1,
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    
    
    geom_label(
        data = letter2word,
        aes(y = from_y), label = "     ", x = 0, fill = "white",
        show.legend = FALSE, size = 6, linewidth = 4/5,
        label.padding = unit(0.1, "lines")
    ) +
    geom_text(
        data = letter2word,
        aes(y = from_y, label = from), x = 0,
        show.legend = FALSE, size = 7
    ) +
    geom_label(
        data = distinct(letter2word, to_y, to),
        aes(y = to_y, label = to), x = 1.5, 
        fill = "white",
        show.legend = FALSE,
        size = 8, linewidth = 4/5
    ) +
    geom_label(
        data = distinct(letter2word, to_y, to),
        aes(y = to_y, label = to, fill = to), x = 1.5,
        alpha = 1/2,
        show.legend = FALSE,
        size = 8, linewidth = 4/5
    ) +
    geom_label(
        data = word2constituent,
        aes(y = to_y, label = to), x = 2.5,
        show.legend = FALSE,
        size = 8, fill = "white", linewidth = 4/5
    )  +

    annotate(
        geom = "text", y = - 14, x = c(0, 1.5, 2.5),
        label = c("letter", "word", "constituent"), size = 10
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(aesthetics = c("fill", "colour"), 
                        values = word_colours, na.value = "gray") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(0, c(0.5, 0.65))) +

    theme_void()



```

We can convince ourselves this same information is captured in the multifactor 
object, `fox`. 
```{r 'show-data', message = FALSE}
levels(fox)

as.matrix(fox$letter2word)
```

# Calculate coverage
## Introduction 
With coverage, we mean the proportion of items in a set that are present. In 
other words, going back to our example, given some number of letters, we can 
calculate which words we can make, and how complete they are. 

To demonstrate, let's first consider the graph representation of our dataset: 
```{r}
#| plot-cov-0, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE,
#| fig.width=10, fig.height=9.25, out.height = "460px", out.width = "500px"
pstart
```

Three feature types are shown on the x-axis, with links between respective 
levels as lines. We can see that each letter is linked to the words it appears 
in, which are in turn linked to their corresponding constituents. 

We'll also need to generate some collection of letters as input data:  
```{r 'setup-example1', message = FALSE}
# Generate some collection of letters
input <- split_to_letters("a pangram is a sentence with all letters")

input
```


## Defining coverage in a path
 
## weave_coverage()
We can use the `weave_coverage()` function to calculate to what degree the input
letters cover the words in our data set. This function behaves similarly to 
`weave()`, in the sense that it takes a multifactor as its first argument, `x`, 
and its second argument, `.path`, defines the path through that multifactor. It 
also has an additional argument, `.data`. 

For now, let's plug in our input letters: 
```{r 'weave-code-specify1', message = FALSE}
res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word ~ constituent, .data = input
)

```

```{r}
#| 'weave-plot-specify1', message=FALSE, echo=FALSE,
#| fig.width=10, fig.height=9.25, out.height = "460px", out.width = "500px", 
#| dev='ragg_png'
psimple
```

### Filter using `subset()`
We can use the `subset()` method for `linkmap` to automatically filter for 
complete cases, only the word 'the' is complete:
```{r subset}
subset(res)
```

By default, coverage is only calculated between the data types involved in the 
last step of the path. However, we can specify conditional filtering steps. 

### Complete coverage
When defining a path, we can use the `:` operator as shorthand for complete 
coverage (`>= 1`). For example: `letter ~ word ~ constituent >= 1` is equivalent 
to `letter ~ word : constituent`. 
```{r 'weave-code-specify2', message = FALSE}
weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word : constituent, .data = input
)
```

```{r }
#| 'weave-plot-specify2', message=FALSE, echo=FALSE,
#| fig.width=10, fig.height=9.25, out.height = "460px", out.width = "500px", 
#| dev='ragg_png'
pdouble
```

### Partial coverage
We can similarly define threshold-based filters using relational expressions. 
For example: `letter ~ word > 0.5 ~ constituent` is equivalent 
to `letter ~ word : constituent`. 
```{r 'weave-code-specify3', message = FALSE}
weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word > 0.5 ~ constituent, .data = input
)
```

```{r }
#| 'weave-plot-specify3', message=FALSE, echo=FALSE,
#| fig.width=10, fig.height=9.25, out.height = "460px", out.width = "500px", 
#| dev='ragg_png'
pthres
```

## Enrichment testing

The `test_enrich()` allows for quick hypothesis testing using the same syntax: 

```{r 'test-enrich1', message = FALSE}
test_enrich(x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input)
```

Alternatively, `test_enrich()` can also be run on the result of an earlier 
`weave_coverage()` call for the same results: 
```{r 'test-enrich2', message = FALSE}
test_enrich(res)
```
